INDEPENDENT PHARMACY RX MARGIN · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Which prescriptions actually make money?

A big reimbursement line is not the same as profit. Type your prescription types, what the patient copay and the PBM each pay, what the drug and supplies cost you, your DIR and post-sale fees, rejection rate, card fees and staff wage. The tool shows what each kind of fill earns, which use a pharmacy staff hour best, the copay that hits your target margin, how insured fills compare with cash fills, and how many prescriptions a month cover your fixed costs.

Arithmetic on the numbers you type. Not tax, legal or financial advice. The values shown are placeholder data, not benchmarks or any real practice's figures.

Your costs

Fees and short-pays withheld from PBM payments.

Share of fills that are rejected, reversed or returned to stock.

Average cost of delivery, counseling and compliance packaging.

Employer taxes, workers' comp, paid breaks.

Rent, utilities, base staffing, pharmacy software, insurance, licenses. Not owner pay.

After drug cost, rework, fees and staff time.

Your prescription types

One row per kind of fill, such as a generic on a commercial plan or a specialty drug. Enter the drug acquisition cost you pay, not the amount billed. Use 0 for PBM pays on a cash fill. Leave a row empty to skip it.

Questions people ask

What is a good margin on a prescription?

Per fill it is thin and it varies enormously by type. A generic on a good commercial plan can earn several dollars after drug cost, supplies, fees and staff time, while a brand or specialty drug on the same plan often passes almost all of its money straight through to the wholesaler and nets a dollar or two. A generic from a low-reimbursement PBM can lose money on every fill. This tool subtracts drug acquisition cost, vials and supplies, PBM claim fees, DIR and post-sale fees, a rework allowance, copay card fees, delivery and the staff's time, then shows what each kind of fill really earns.

How do PBM reimbursements and DIR fees change the math?

A PBM pays a contracted amount per claim and the patient pays a copay on top. Fees charged after the sale, often called DIR fees, can claw back part of it weeks later. Enter the copay, what the PBM pays, and your DIR and post-sale fees per fill as separate numbers. The card fee applies only to the copay and the claim fee only to the PBM payment, and the tool gives you the copay that would reach your target margin if the PBM payment is fixed.

What does a rejected claim cost?

A rejected or reversed claim costs the vial and supplies again plus staff time to call, resubmit or restock. Multiply by how often it happens. Even a four percent rework rate quietly takes cents from every fill, and the scenario table shows what three more points would cost across a month.

How many prescriptions a month do I need to cover fixed costs?

Divide monthly fixed costs (rent, utilities, base staffing, pharmacy software, insurance, licenses) by the average contribution per fill at your current mix of generics, brands, cash and specialty fills. The result is only as good as that mix, so rerun it if a PBM changes its rates or you add a specialty line.

Not decided

What your market will pay, which PBM networks to join, your contracted rates and DIR terms, wholesaler and buying-group terms, 340B and compliance questions, controlled-substance handling, the pharmacist-in-charge's compensation, and how to treat any of this for tax or accounting. Take costs from wholesaler invoices, take payments and fees from your remittance advices, and talk to your accountant about the books. No patient names or prescription data belong in this page and it never asks for them.

Everything runs in your browser. Your answers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (analysis_run, example_loaded, report_downloaded) are counted only in your browser's local storage, honour Do Not Track, and can be switched off below.
